today.critic_reason: Repeats the dropped family "Price pressure around the crypto perpetuals' funding times (00:00, 08:00 and 16:00 UTC)". The cited evidence (arXiv 2411.06327) also already appears in the dropped family "Exchange flows of USDT and BTC as intraday signals (arXiv 2411.06327)". No genuinely new evidence is offered for an already archived funding-time price-pressure family.
today.data_source: Binance USDT‑M perpetual contract data (2023‑2025) – price and funding rate series.
today.duplicate_of: Price pressure around the crypto perpetuals' funding times (00:00, 08:00 and 16:00 UTC)
today.evidence: arXiv 2411.06327 (2024) documented order‑flow imbalance and price impact at funding times for Binance USDT‑M perpetuals.
today.mechanism: Traders are forced to roll or adjust leveraged positions at the three daily funding timestamps (00:00, 08:00, 16:00 UTC). The abrupt change in funding rate creates temporary supply‑demand imbalance, causing price drift that can be captured by taking opposite sides of the drift.
today.rule: At each funding timestamp, if the 8‑hour funding rate exceeds +0.01 % (long pressure) or is below –0.01 % (short pressure), open a market order for a fixed 15‑minute position (size = 1 % of account equity) in the direction of the pressure, then close the position at the next funding timestamp or when a 0.5 % profit/loss is reached, whichever occurs first. No look‑ahead data is used.
today.title: Funding‑time price pressure in Binance USDT‑M perpetuals
today.why: Repeats the dropped family "Price pressure around the crypto perpetuals' funding times (00:00, 08:00 and 16:00 UTC)". The cited evidence (arXiv 2411.06327) also already appears in the dropped family "Exchange flows of USDT and BTC as intraday signals (arXiv 2411.06327)". No genuinely new evidence is offered for an already archived funding-time price-pressure family.
today.why_new: The mechanism exploits the documented forced position adjustments at funding timestamps, a timing effect not previously tested in any of the 138 archived strategies; the evidence comes from a recent paper measuring order‑flow at those exact times, which the lab has not used.

today.critic_reason: Repeats the dropped family "Retail-broker client positioning as a contrarian signal (the share of a broker's clients long the US 500 or gold, read against them)". Restricting the same contrarian client-ratio signal to monthly options-expiration weeks is a variant of an already dropped family, not genuinely new evidence; it also overlaps dropped options-expiration week families.
today.data_source: Broker client position data (e.g., from a retail CFD broker) for US equity ETFs, weekly frequency, 2023‑2025.
today.duplicate_of: Retail-broker client positioning as a contrarian signal
today.evidence: Retail‑broker client positioning as a contrarian signal (paper presented at the 2022 Quantitative Finance Conference) measured weekly long‑ratio for US equity ETFs; the lab has not yet applied this filter to expiration weeks.
today.mechanism: Retail investors tend to overweight popular ETFs (e.g., SPY, QQQ) as the monthly options expiration approaches, creating excess demand that is unwound after expiration, producing a predictable price rebound that benefits traders who take the opposite side.
today.rule: At the start of the trading week that contains the monthly options expiration (the week with the third Friday), if the broker‑client long‑position ratio for the ETF exceeds 70 % (based on publicly available client position data), purchase the ETF at the market open of that Monday and hold until the close of the expiration Friday; then sell the position. If the long‑ratio is below 30 %, short the ETF on Monday and cover on Friday. Position size = 1 % of equity per trade.
today.title: Retail client contrarian during monthly options expiration weeks in US equity ETFs
today.why: Repeats the dropped family "Retail-broker client positioning as a contrarian signal (the share of a broker's clients long the US 500 or gold, read against them)". Restricting the same contrarian client-ratio signal to monthly options-expiration weeks is a variant of an already dropped family, not genuinely new evidence; it also overlaps dropped options-expiration week families.
today.why_new: The hypothesis uses the documented client‑position contrarian effect but applies it specifically to the weekly window around monthly options expirations, a subset never examined in the lab’s prior work; the evidence is the weekly client‑ratio series that the lab has not yet incorporated.

today.critic_reason: Repeats the rejected family "EIA crude oil inventory surprise same-day mean reversion (REJECTED_BY_CRITIC)". Reframing the same EIA-surprise energy-futures event as a 5-day near/next-month calendar spread does not constitute genuinely new evidence; the underlying family and data source were already rejected.
today.data_source: EIA weekly crude oil inventory reports (2023‑2025) and corresponding CME energy futures prices (continuous contract chain).
today.duplicate_of: EIA crude oil inventory surprise same-day mean reversion
today.evidence: EIA inventory surprise series (U.S. Energy Information Administration) combined with CME futures price data; the lab has not previously examined the near‑month/next‑month spread reaction to these surprises.
today.mechanism: When the EIA crude oil inventory report shows a larger‑than‑expected surprise, hedge funds and other leveraged participants must rapidly adjust their futures exposure, causing a temporary widening of the price spread between near‑month and next‑month contracts. This spread reverts, offering a risk‑free profit to traders who are long the near‑month and short the next‑month.
today.rule: On any day where the EIA inventory change deviates from the consensus forecast by more than 0.5 % (positive or negative), calculate the fair value of the near‑month/next‑month spread using the previous day’s term‑structure. If the observed spread deviates by more than 5 bps from fair value, open a calendar‑spread position: buy the near‑month contract and sell the next‑month contract, with each leg sized at 0.5 % of equity. Hold the spread for five trading days, then close both legs at the market close on the fifth day. No look‑ahead data beyond the report release is used.
today.title: EIA inventory surprise term‑structure premium in energy futures
today.why: Repeats the rejected family "EIA crude oil inventory surprise same-day mean reversion (REJECTED_BY_CRITIC)". Reframing the same EIA-surprise energy-futures event as a 5-day near/next-month calendar spread does not constitute genuinely new evidence; the underlying family and data source were already rejected.
today.why_new: The mechanism relies on the documented forced rebalancing of futures positions after large inventory surprises, a relationship not yet tested in the lab’s energy‑futures studies; the fresh data includes the full 2023‑2025 inventory series and continuous futures chain.
